results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 34 aligned units match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph in the spec's order; the three opening callouts match no spec paragraph by house format. The summary of Testing the Strategy ¶2 (p18) covers the mapping and its being the author's, but not 'shows where such a strategy can be empty', which the draft does not state in words; the idea is otherwise intact.

Three units were marked two_ideas. Introduction ¶2 is thesis plus roadmap, one unit by the spec's design (p02). What AI Changes Here ¶1 opens with the label scheme by house rule and then holds one Emerging claim (p26). Strategy Works Backward ¶3 (p13) covers the sequencing factors and the milestones, which the spec's single controlling idea joins and the draft's last sentence unifies ('the order of the steps is also the order of the outcomes'); judged one idea.

Every unit ties to the supporting claim its section declares (S1 to S5); the AI units to S2 and S3. The one-sentence Chapter 2 aside in Pattern: Write the Vision ¶1 is a cross-reference inside a paragraph that traces to S2.

Each quotation is introduced or followed by a sentence saying what it shows; the three-visions table and the kernel table are framed by lead-ins that state what they compare, the journey table and the steps table are each followed by a paragraph that reads the three requests against them, Figure 1 has an explaining caption, and the 2026 planning figure is followed by what it separates.

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary with the declared carried-over information, including the conclusion's label phrases and the hand-off to roadmaps-and-horizons. What AI Changes Here ¶2 opens with a parallel ('Cheaper drawing has a counterpart in cheaper building') and states the declared cause and effect in the next two sentences; accepted.

Terms are defined at first use (end-state vision, customer journey vision, planner, route optimization, point A and B, kernel, hallmarks, product principles, message brokers); labels and Corvane are explained by the book's introduction. No term of art is used before it is known. The unexplained 'planner's trust' principle is a flow matter and is recorded under flow_is_followable.
Opens on a specific scenario, bridges from the reader's own meeting, states a disputable thesis and a roadmap; none of the weak patterns.
Sorted by how settled each point is; no new subtopic, no body evidence, does not end on a rephrased thesis alone but on the callback and the hand-off.

What to Take Away ¶3 states what no single section states (vision and strategy do different jobs and fail differently; both are needed before one outcome can be chosen over another), and the closing paragraph says what the reader can now do with a request.
The closing paragraph returns to the three requests of 2025 and the three answers: no, not yet, yes in a narrower form.

The cold reader's predicted order (three requests, vision defined and written, strategy defined and three steps, Rumelt's test, disagreements, hand-on to engineering strategy and planning, AI), evidence (Corvane case plus named authorities) and tone match the roadmap's six promises.
The cold reader picked (b) as the vision (the customer's future journey), (a) as an ambition or mission statement and (c) as a feature list, as expected.

What the Product Strategy Hands On states both relations (product strategy tells engineering what must become true and receives constraints; it tells planning which outcomes come first and planning decides capacity) and links [[engineering-strategy]] and [[planning]], naming Part IV and Part VI.

Build What Matters, Good Strategy Bad Strategy and Empowered are named with their concepts; the three-year horizon is given as 'their rule of thumb and not a law'; the recognizability test, the outcome measure, the three-step limit, the refusal, the kernel mapping and the steps-plus-problems combination are each marked as the author's; Cagan is declared as read through the author's summaries.

Both patterns name their users (the people who answer requests; product leaders who answer requests and brief teams) and outcome measures (share of requests answered by pointing to a stage; milestones reached at reassessment and requests escalated per quarter).

results.draft_locus: Pattern: Three Steps, Each with a Milestone and a No ¶3
results.quote: One principle sets that order: earn the planner's trust one disruption at a time before planning the whole week.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated this (a). Reader A: the previous section said order comes from prerequisites and six sequencing factors; 'this principle is none of them and arrives unexplained', and turns out later to be the guiding policy, 'a part of a strategy the definition section never mentioned'. Reader B: 'Trust has not been named as a problem'; went back to the steps section to find where it had been established. The spec's flow has each definition precede the Corvane artifact written to it; here the artifact uses an ordering principle that neither the definition section (p11 to p13b) nor the gap paragraph (p14b) prepares. The draft renders p15's lead-in as the spec words it, so the gap is in the spec; one sentence in the gap paragraph or the lead-in saying why trust is the obstacle would close it without changing the order.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3 (rated a); primary: flow reader A, item 1 (rated a)
results.waived_by: Author (Željko Obrenović), 2026-11-19, decision 'waive by rule' under the rule 'max two rounds per chapter': this finding remained after the last check round allowed. It was listed in the writer's report to the author; where the writer revised the unit afterwards, the revision was not re-checked by fresh readers, and where the writer left the unit unchanged, the finding stands as written.

results.quote: The three steps name the obstacle, which is that the planner's knowledge is not held as data, and each of them refuses something.
results.finding: Both flow readers rated this (a). Reader A went back to the steps table: the cause 'appears only inside step 2's prerequisite cell, and the earlier gap paragraph ("That was the gap") does not give this cause. The diagnosis seems to appear first in the test.' Reader B: the cause 'appears first inside a table cell of step 2 and is called the diagnosis only in the kernel section. I went back to the steps section'. The spec says p14b gives 'the later diagnosis its content', but its controlling idea and the draft's gap paragraph give only the symptom (cannot propose a schedule), not the cause. Same root as the ordering-principle finding; stating the cause in the point A paragraph would fix both.
